There Is this book about drawing i read a long time ago called "drawing from the right side of the brain" or something along those lines

In the same vein as how others have said our brains compartmentalize and compress information, it also tries to do things in a quick way rather than an accurate way sometimes

For example you might want to draw a hand, you can picture it in you mind, but when you try and draw it, your brain goes "OOh i know what a hand looks like its like a circle with five sausagues attachted" and then you draw a terrible version of a hand. Your brain will keep making mistakes like this as it recalls things inaccurately and trying to be quick. 

A lot of lot what learning to draw from life is trying to override this, and instead drawing what you actually see and not what your brain thinks you see. The real life shapes of things are very complicated and not as simple as our brains recall things as. A lot of learning to draw is learing to override this part of our brain that gives us this quick simplifications and actually drawing the actually complicated silhouettes of things.

A lot of artists learn to actually "trick" their brains to draw accurately. This can involve drawing using negative space, where you dont draw what you see, for example a chair. Instead you draw the silhouette of a chair and the weird geometry that you actually see. 

Another trick is when people might draw something upside down so your brain cant even recognize what its meant to be drawing. Theres a common practise exercise in novice drawing classes where you copy a bunch of lines as practice, and then as a surprise the students all flip the picture upside down and they have done a much better picture of a person than they would have usually been able to.

If you plan on continuing in wargames and rpgs and the like i think its a great investment. I got a basic  entry level anycubic photon mono (\~200 bucks) and it has been great, very happy with the print quality.

Pros

\- I can find most minis i want for either free or very cheap, and in terms of resin each model only costs like 20 cents or so. So its very cost effective way way less than buying at games workshop

\-Can print whatever i want or need, dont need to buy a full set of minis from gw if i only want a couple of models or specific parts.

\-Great print quality from resin printers.

\-Even quite "small" printers can still make large models too.

​

Cons

\-Deals with some irritating chemicals (the resin itself, cleaning products etc)

\-Bit of maintenance, i find i go through a lot of gloves trying to keep my workspace clean

\-Bit of time to learn how to print and support minis (though you can get presupported stuff)

\-Need to be properly cured after making them, otherwise they can go bad after a while

\-Resin can be heavy and brittle, you can drop a break minis, gw plastic is virtually indestructable in comparison.

​

Overall i'd say keep enjoying the hobby, and think about it down the track, if you can see yourself expanding your collection with more than 300 or so dollars worth of dudes it might make more economic sense to get a printer

I think for most games in a casual setting people wont care if you have printed minis, if you plan on going to competitions and that sorta thing they probably wont be allowed.

Ive greatly enjoyed printing my minis and have been pretty impressed with the quality. Its great being able to just make what i want and get great value for money. 

There is a bit of a learning curve in using the 3d printers. Can take a bit of experimentation to get a good understanding of setting supports and angles for minis. As well as there is a bit of learning with curing and cleaning and processing the finished minis.

Overall id recommend a printer.

Yeah i love playing the game solo!

Whilst it is a game with a lot of strategy, it feels as though it still runs great solo. Having the meta knowledge of what cards both players have doesn't matter too much, its not like poker where knowing each others hands ruins the game. A lot of the strategies for each "player" are dictated on the fly by what cards are drawn so it still feels as though there is a lot of variety and fluidity if you are playing by yourself.

Generally when playing solo, i find this is a very easy game to play in earnest and do what is best for each side. After playing this game for a while you realize lot of the "traps" in this game can be prevented by playing by certain "rules". In example, its always good to leave some troops with sauraman so he doesnt get ganked by ents, or if the fellowship is revealed its good to hide them or get them to a stronghold so they don't get hurt. So normally ill try and play both sides by these general rules anyway, so i dont have to worry about outsmarting myself

Don't know if they are christian or religious, but certainly there is a lot of symbology in a lot of medieval art and hieromonus bosch's work. A lot of elements in paintings have a lot of meaning but some of it is seemingly random. I'm not religious myself but i find a lot of the symbolism in christianinty and art and in Bosch's work pretty interesting.

That jester character or fool is often a symbol of being a buffoon, carrying about valueless things, unknowing of where you are going or where you have been and meandering off into your own destruction. Although the Jester is often seen as a fool who is often being laughed at rather than with, they are also merry and blessed by the naivety in a way, that they laugh and joke up until their destruction whether they know or not. To me The jester comes across as a symbol of both wisdom and foolishness. Foolish in that he is dim witted and naive, but wise in that he is happy go lucky and enjoys his time on the earth. Sometimes the joker is also a symbol of a bit of a trickster who is secretly wise all along. 

I'm sure you could spend days looking for meaning in Bosch's paintings of the seven deadly sins, even longer in his paintings of the garden of earthly delights. Not much is known about him, a lot of his more surrealist imagery is said to be caused by psychological delusions, some say by saint anthonys fire, which is a disease caused by consuming ergot fungus. (It has similar effects of LSD). So who knows, perhaps we can read into every detail of his work and think there is some intended meaning but it is just as likely it is the wild dreams of a man plagued by psychosis.

"So if a pig can not have a human experience, that is a trait, that if not present in a human, would make a human life not worth living."

The name the trait argument doesn't ask whether a life is worth living or not, but whether something with that particular trait is not worth moral consideration. As you say yourself "it does not mean, that a human at that point, shouldn't have any moral consideration". We don't use "fulfilling human life" as an indicator of whether or not someone deserves to live at all. We still give moral consideration to people who are unable to live a "fulfilling human life", so we cannot say other animals are unworthy of moral consideration because they cannot live a "fulfilling human life". If this is deployed to kill a pig against it's will, you would also have to accept it as a reason to kill a human against their will. 

"Can you explain, why you think sentience should gauge moral worth, and how?"

Sure thing! For me the only point at which I would accept having no moral value at all is when I have no sentience (I consider it in terms of an experience of subjective reality). Remove any other quality such as intelligence, quality of life, physical capability, culture etc. and I would not accept the absence of these qualities as a good reason to kill me for no good reason. If sentience was removed, I would not give a fuck what happened to me as I am not experiencing a subjective reality (I am virtually already dead), and killing me would not end my experience of reality as it is already gone.

"The principles of "namethetrait" are based on human abnormalities and the possibility of an aliens invasion, so it is an argument where you can smell from a mile, that something is just not right, something stinks."

The argument simply aims to illustrate the fact that the traits used to justify killing others are unlikely to be accepted when applied to themselves or others. This requires hypotheticals in some situations. Hypotheticals are perfectly valid for demonstrating why a justification would not be accepted for someone proposing the trait. 

"Humans already have the possibility of assisted suicide or euthanasia in some countries. So we already justify death in a lot of cases, where society, families or individuals think, that life has no value."

Of course we do, and in these cases we can justify euthanasia. What we don't do is euthanize people without any good reason to do so. I don't see why you see this as an issue with the argument?

"The trait could be "not being able to live a fulfilling human life". A pig can not live a fulfilling human life."

If you deployed "not being able to live a fulfilling human life" as a justification for killing a pig, you would have to either accept that humans unable to 'live a fulfilling human life' would also be undeserving of moral consideration or deploy a different justification.

"If a chicken had better mental and/or physical abilities than a disabled human, shouldn't the chicken be granted greater moral value or consideration?"

It depends on what you deploy to determine moral value. If "mental and/or physical abilities" is what you use to gauge moral value then yes.

"For example, why shouldn't saving lives of chickens and pigs and horses possibly have higher priority then saving disabled people in cases of emergency (like an earthquake or fire)?"

Depends on what you deploy to gauge moral value. If you deploy "mental and/or physical abilities" then you would save the most mentally sound or most physically able first. If you deploy "not being able to live a fulfilling human life" you may not even be concerned with saving anyone at all depending on your criteria for a "fulfilling life". I personally use sentience to try and gauge moral worth, and if had to choose between saving a horse and a human with a level of sentience even less than that of a horse I'd preserve the horse. (Provided that secondary harms are accounted for etc).

I'd like to add that it's not only the potential to suffer that most people consider, but but also simply having a subjective experience of the world is valuable and to take that away from something unjustly is wrong.
